```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 6.5,
  fig.height = 4.5, dpi = 144, out.width = "100%", dev = "svglite", fig.ext = "svg",
  dev.args = list(pointsize = 14))
PAL <- c(blue = "#2E6F9E", red = "#B5342B", green = "#3F7A3D",
         orange = "#9E5E0F", purple = "#7A4F9E", teal = "#2A7A7A",
         grey = "#5C6166")
library(ggplot2)
library(ggplot3d)
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 17) + theme(
  plot.background = element_rect(fill = "transparent", colour = NA),
  panel.background = element_rect(fill = "transparent", colour = NA),
  legend.background = element_rect(fill = "transparent", colour = NA),
  legend.key = element_rect(fill = "transparent", colour = NA),
  legend.box.background = element_rect(fill = "transparent", colour = NA),
  legend.position = "none"))
```

A document can display a 3D plot as a static figure or an interactive viewer.
This article uses knitr's output switching, supplies accessible descriptions
and arranges plots on a page. Quarto's R engine uses the same chunk options.
Installation is covered in [Get started](ggplot3d.html); HTML viewers also
need [htmlwidgets](https://www.htmlwidgets.org/) and
[svglite](https://svglite.r-lib.org/), described in [Interactive viewing](viewer.html).

## A static figure

The motor-car data record weight in thousands of pounds, fuel economy in
miles per US gallon and gross horsepower. Printing the plot uses its chosen
scene backend and the document's graphics device. The default backend draws
vector geometry; this article's SVG device keeps those paths scalable.

```{r static, fig.alt="Motor cars positioned by weight, fuel economy and horsepower, with higher-power cars toward the upper part of the box."}
p <- ggplot(mtcars, aes(wt, mpg, z = hp)) +
  geom_point_3d(size = 3, colour = PAL["blue"]) + coord_3d() +
  labs(x = "weight", y = "mpg", z = "horsepower")
p
```

## HTML, PDF and Word

Set the chunk option `view3d = TRUE` to embed the interactive viewer in HTML.
The following chunk runs that switch. The figure dimensions are in inches,
and become widget dimensions at 96 pixels per inch. Facet panels, titles,
strips and legends follow the plot's layout. Set `fig.asp = NULL` to keep
the explicit dimensions when the document supplies a default figure aspect
ratio, as pkgdown does. An automatic ratio can produce fractional pixel
dimensions, which the viewer currently rejects.

```{r interactive, view3d=TRUE, fig.width=6.5, fig.height=4.5, fig.asp=NULL, fig.alt="Interactive motor-car scatterplot with weight, fuel economy and horsepower axes."}
p
```

For PDF and Word output, that same option draws a static vector scene.
The document device determines the image format: a PDF device retains vector
geometry for a PDF document, and a PNG device samples it into pixels for Word.
With `view3d = FALSE`, the chunk uses the backend configured on the plot.

Quarto accepts the equivalent option in its cell metadata. This is the same
plot object created above.

````markdown
```{r}
#| view3d: true
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 4.5
#| fig-asp: null
#| fig-alt: "Motor cars by weight, fuel economy and horsepower."
p
```
````

## Accessible descriptions

`alt_text_3d()` describes the layer types, mapped variables and initial camera
angles. The generated description supplies the default alternative text for
static figures and an accessible group name around HTML viewers. Inspect it
before adding words about what the figure communicates.

```{r description}
alt_text_3d(p)
```

An explicit chunk `fig.alt` takes precedence. A description supplied by
`labs(alt = ...)` takes precedence over the generated layer description.
The example below describes the relationship the reader can inspect in the
motor-car plot.

```{r explicit-description}
described <- p + labs(alt = paste(
  "Motor cars plotted by weight, fuel economy and horsepower.",
  "Heavier cars generally have lower fuel economy."))
alt_text_3d(described)
```

When a chunk prints several plots, supply a vector of descriptions in their
printed order. Each static figure gets its own alternative text.

```{r several-plots, fig.alt=c("Motor cars seen from azimuth minus sixty degrees.", "The same motor cars seen from azimuth thirty degrees.")}
p
p + coord_3d(azimuth = 30)
```

## Composing plots

[patchwork](https://patchwork.data-imaginist.com/) arranges ggplot objects.
Each 3D scene compiles at the physical size of its panel, so camera projection
and mark sizes follow the final layout. Stack the plot above a second view
to give each one the document column's width.

```{r patchwork, fig.height=8, fig.alt="Two motor-car plots stacked vertically with different camera angles."}
other <- p + coord_3d(azimuth = 30)
patchwork::wrap_plots(p, other, ncol = 1)
```

[cowplot](https://wilkelab.org/cowplot/) also preserves the independent scenes.
Its composition below contains a 3D view and a 2D view of the same cars.
These arrangements are static figures; use a faceted ggplot with the
viewer for a live multi-panel document.

```{r cowplot, fig.height=8, fig.alt="A 3D motor-car plot above a 2D scatterplot of weight and fuel economy."}
flat <- ggplot(mtcars, aes(wt, mpg)) +
  geom_point(colour = PAL["blue"], size = 3) + labs(x = "weight", y = "mpg")
cowplot::plot_grid(p, flat, ncol = 1)
```

[Combining 2D and 3D graphics](combining-2d-3d.html) shows shared scales and
plots placed on planes inside a scene.

## Saving a raster figure

Choose the scene sampling resolution on the backend, then set the saved
image's pixel dimensions through the device resolution. Both settings use
the intended physical size. The temporary file below is
six inches wide and four inches high at 144 dots per inch.

```{r save}
raster <- p + coord_3d(backend = backend_3d("raster", dpi = 144))
path <- tempfile(fileext = ".png")
ggsave(path, raster, width = 6, height = 4, dpi = 144)
file.info(path)$size > 0
unlink(path)
```

[Output backends](backends.html) explains the rendering choices.
[Exporting plots and scenes](export.html) writes model files and native SVG,
TikZ or Asymptote output.
